title: Nature and Scope of Business
summary: Economic activities are done to earn money or a living — a shopkeeper selling goods, a teacher teaching in a school for a salary, a factory worker. Non-economic activities are done out of love, affection, religious feeling, social obligation or for recreation, not for money — a mother cooking for the family, charity, playing games, teaching one's own child. The same activity can be economic at one time and non-economic at another: a doctor treating patients in a clinic is economic; treating her own child is not. They differ in purpose (money vs satisfaction), outcome (income and wealth vs personal satisfaction) and expectation (return vs none).

An occupation is an economic activity in which a person is regularly engaged to earn a living. Three types: (1) Employment — working regularly for another (employer) for a fixed income (wages or salary) under terms and conditions decided by the employer. (2) Profession — rendering specialised personal services that need special knowledge and training, for a fee; e.g. doctor, lawyer, chartered accountant, engineer. A profession is regulated by a professional body (Medical Council, Bar Council, ICAI) that lays down a code of conduct; little capital is needed. (3) Business — regular production or purchase of goods and services for sale with the aim of earning profit. Business itself is not a profession.

Business is an activity involving regular production or purchase of goods and services for sale, transfer or exchange with the object of earning profit. Characteristics: (1) dealing in goods and services; (2) sale, transfer or exchange — a cobbler making shoes for himself is not doing business; (3) regularity of dealings — a single sale of rare books to a friend is not business; (4) profit motive; (5) investment of capital; (6) risk and uncertainty of return; (7) consumer satisfaction; (8) creativity and innovation.

Economic objectives: earning profit; creating customers; regular innovation; best possible use of resources (materials, machines, money and people). Social objectives: supplying goods of desired quality at fair prices; avoiding unfair practices such as hoarding, black marketing and misleading advertisements; generating employment; paying taxes honestly; welfare of society. Human objectives: economic well-being and fair treatment of employees, their participation in management, development of skills, and opportunities for differently-abled people. National objectives: generating employment, promoting social justice, producing according to national priorities, contributing to government revenue, self-sufficiency and export promotion. Global objectives: raising the general standard of living, reducing disparities among nations, and making competitive goods available worldwide.

Social responsibility means all the duties of business towards the welfare of society. Business needs it because it creates goodwill, helps long-term survival and growth, satisfies employees (and so raises productivity), and because consumers are aware of their rights. Business has responsibilities to interest groups: owners (fair return, safety of investment, accurate information); investors (safety of money, regular return, honest information); employees (fair wages, safe working conditions, welfare facilities, recognition); suppliers (regular orders, timely payment, fair terms); customers (quality goods and services at reasonable prices, honest advertising, after-sales service, quick handling of complaints); competitors (fair competition); government (obeying laws, paying taxes honestly); society (protecting the environment, helping weaker sections, preserving culture).

Pollution is contamination of the environment by substances harmful to living and non-living things. Air pollution — from factory smoke, vehicles, burning of fuels — causes breathing diseases and acid rain. Water pollution — from human excreta and sewage drained into rivers, poor sanitation, industrial effluents and fertiliser and pesticide run-off — spreads diseases and kills aquatic life. Land pollution — from solid wastes of industries, mines and quarries, plastic bags and excess fertilisers and pesticides — reduces fertility. Business can play three roles in controlling pollution: preventive (using clean technology, treating waste before disposal), curative (cleaning up damage it has caused, planting trees) and awareness (educating employees and the public about pollution).

objective: Write True (T) or False (F): (a) It is not always necessary for a businessman to make the best possible use of materials. (b) Businessmen should use profits only for their own living.

(a) False — best use of resources is an economic objective of business.
(b) False — profits should also be ploughed back for growth and used for the welfare of employees and society.

Fill in the blanks: (a) The economic activity in which one is regularly engaged is called his/her ________. (b) The occupation in which people work for others and earn a fixed income is called ________.
Fill in the blanks: (a) Activities performed with the objective of earning money are known as ________ activities. (b) The terms and conditions of employment are decided by the ________.

Fill in the blanks: (a) Today, because of ________, the whole world has become a big market. (b) Paying taxes to the government honestly and regularly is a responsibility of business towards the ________.
Give an example of an activity which at one time is economic and at another time non-economic.

(a) A doctor treating patients in her clinic for a fee — economic.
(b) The same doctor treating her own child at home — non-economic.
Write True (T) or False (F): (a) A profession requires specialised knowledge and training. (b) Regularity of dealings is not necessary for an activity to be called business.

(a) True
(b) False — business requires regular dealings.
vsa: Mamta sold some rare books to a friend for ₹4,000 and made a profit of ₹1,000. Can this be called business?
No. Business needs regularity of dealings. Mamta sold the books only once, so although she earned a profit, it is not business.
Explain the term 'profession' and give two examples.

A profession is an occupation that renders specialised personal services which need special knowledge and training, for a fee, and is regulated by a professional body with a code of conduct. Examples: doctor (Medical Council), lawyer (Bar Council), chartered accountant (ICAI).
What is meant by social objectives of business? State any two.

Social objectives are the goals business pursues for the benefit of society. Any two: supplying quality goods at fair prices; avoiding unfair practices like hoarding and misleading advertising; generating employment; paying taxes honestly.

or: State any three responsibilities of business towards investors.
Ensuring the safety of their money; giving a regular and fair return; giving true and timely information about the company's financial position and plans.

vsa: Give two examples each of economic and non-economic activities.

Economic: a teacher teaching in a school for a salary; a shopkeeper selling goods.
Non-economic: a mother cooking for her family; a person doing charity or social service.
How can business control pollution? Explain two of its roles.

Preventive role: use clean technology and treat smoke and effluents before release so that pollution does not occur.
Curative role: repair the damage already caused — clean up rivers and land, plant trees.
(Awareness role: educate employees and the public about pollution.)
State any three responsibilities of business towards creditors (suppliers).
Giving regular orders; making payment on time; dealing with them fairly and honestly (fair terms, no undue pressure).
sa: State any three features of business.

(1) Dealing in goods and services — producing or buying them for sale. (2) Regularity — dealings must be regular, not a one-time sale. (3) Profit motive — the main aim is to earn profit. (4) Risk and uncertainty — the return is never certain. (Any three.)

What is business? Explain any two characteristics of business.

Business is a regular activity of producing or buying goods and services for sale, transfer or exchange with the object of earning profit.
(1) Sale or exchange: goods are produced for others — making for oneself is not business.
(2) Risk and uncertainty: a businessman invests capital but the return is uncertain because of changes in demand, competition, etc.

or: What is water pollution? Explain any two causes.

Water pollution is contamination of water by unwanted and harmful substances that make it unfit for use.
Causes: (1) drainage of human excreta and sewage into rivers and canals; (2) dumping of industrial wastes and effluents; (3) run-off of fertilisers, chemicals and pesticides from fields. (Any two.)

sa: Differentiate between economic and non-economic activities on the basis of purpose, outcome and expectation.

Purpose: economic activities aim to earn money; non-economic activities aim at satisfaction (love, social or religious feeling).
Outcome: economic activities produce income and wealth; non-economic activities give personal satisfaction.
Expectation: in economic activities a monetary return is expected; in non-economic activities no return is expected.

(1) Social/charitable — helping flood victims, blood donation.
(2) Religious — visiting a temple, serving at a gurdwara langar.
(3) Family and personal — a mother cooking for the family, playing games for recreation.

What is air pollution? State three impacts of it.

Air pollution is contamination of the air by smoke, dust and harmful gases from factories, vehicles and burning of fuels.
Impacts: breathing diseases such as asthma and bronchitis; acid rain that damages buildings and crops; global warming and climate change.

Explain the preventive and curative role of business in controlling environmental pollution.

Preventive: avoid pollution at the source — use clean fuels and technology, install treatment plants for waste water and filters for smoke, follow pollution laws.
Curative: undo damage already done — clean polluted rivers and land, plant trees, recycle waste.
(Awareness: educate employees and the public.)
October 2019
la: Explain any four economic objectives of business.

(1) Earning profit — profit is essential for survival and growth and is the reward for risk.
(2) Creating customers — profit comes only when goods are sold, so business must attract and satisfy customers by offering the right products at the right price.
(3) Regular innovation — introducing new products, designs and methods to cut costs and beat competition.
(4) Best possible use of resources — using men, materials, machines and money efficiently so that nothing is wasted and costs stay low.
What are national objectives of business? Explain four of them.

National objectives are goals business pursues for the progress of the country.
(1) Generating employment for the people.
(2) Promoting social justice — equal opportunity to all, help to weaker sections.
(3) Producing according to national priorities — goods needed by the nation, as in the plans.
(4) Contributing to government revenue by paying taxes honestly; also self-sufficiency and export promotion.
Explain any four responsibilities of business towards owners, and any three towards employees.

Owners: (1) a fair return on their investment; (2) safety of their capital; (3) efficient and honest management; (4) accurate and timely information about the business.
Employees: (1) fair wages and salaries on time; (2) safe and healthy working conditions; (3) welfare facilities, training and chances of promotion.
Distinguish between business, profession and employment on any five bases.

Mode of establishment: business — entrepreneur's decision and legal formalities; profession — membership of a professional body; employment — appointment letter.
Nature of work: business — goods and services to the public; profession — specialised personal services; employment — work as assigned by the employer.
Qualification: business — none required; profession — special knowledge and training; employment — as prescribed by the employer.
Reward: business — profit; profession — fee; employment — salary or wages.
Capital: business — needed as per size; profession — limited; employment — none.
Risk: business — high; profession — low; employment — none.
Explain any three social and any three global objectives of business.

Social: (1) supplying goods of desired quality at fair prices; (2) avoiding unfair trade practices such as hoarding and misleading advertisements; (3) generating employment and contributing to social welfare.
Global: (1) raising the general standard of living by making quality goods available; (2) reducing disparities among nations through trade and investment; (3) making globally competitive goods and services available.
